# Spec: byte sizes that round up to 1000 (or 1024) must move to the next unit

## Context

The byte-size formatters of this Go module choose the unit from the exact value and then round the number they
print. Close below a unit boundary the rounding carries the number up to the base, and the output shows a number
that should have been written with the next unit:

- `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.0 MB"`;
- `IBytes(1_048_575)` (1 MiB − 1) returns `"1024 KiB"` instead of `"1.0 MiB"`;
- `BigBytes(big.NewInt(999_999))` returns `"1000 kB"`, `BigIBytes` of 1 MiB − 1 returns `"1024 KiB"`;
- `BytesN(999_999, 3)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.00 MB"`.

The formatters are in `bytes.go` (`Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`, helper `humanateBytes`) and `bigbytes.go`
(`BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`, helper `humanateBigBytes`). Tests are next to them (`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`);
some existing test cases currently expect the wrong outputs above (for example `"1000 kB"` for `MByte - Byte`).

## Goal

No byte formatter prints a number equal to or larger than its base when a larger unit exists; such values are
printed exactly as the value of one unit of the next size is printed.

## Functional requirements

FR1. For `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN` (any `n`), `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes`: when the number that the function would
print, after its own rounding, is greater than or equal to the base (1000 for SI, 1024 for IEC) and the function's
unit list has a larger unit, the result is the string that the same function returns for exactly one of that
larger unit. Examples: `Bytes(999_999) == Bytes(1_000_000) == "1.0 MB"`; `Bytes(999_500) == "1.0 MB"`;
`IBytes(1_048_575) == "1.0 MiB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 3) == "1.00 MB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 0) == BytesN(1_000_000, 0)`;
`BigBytes` of 10⁹ − 1 `== "1.0 GB"`; `BigIBytes` of 1 GiB − 1 `== "1.0 GiB"`.

FR2. Every other output is unchanged. In particular values whose rounded number stays below the base keep their
current output: `Bytes(999_499) == "999 kB"`, `IBytes(1000 * 1024) == "1000 KiB"`, `IBytes(1023 * 1024) == "1023 KiB"`,
and all outputs for values below 10 bytes.

FR3. There is no unit after the last one: for the largest unit of a function (`QB` and `QiB` for the `Big`
functions) the number is printed as today, even when it is 1000 (or 1024) or more.

FR4. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` still do not modify the `*big.Int` they receive.

FR5. The existing test cases that encode the wrong outputs of the Context are corrected to the new outputs, and new
test cases cover FR1 to FR4 for each of the five functions, including the exact boundary values (the smallest input
that is promoted and the largest one that is not).

FR6. The doc comments of the five functions stay correct; if an example in a doc comment or in `README.markdown`
shows one of the wrong outputs, it is corrected.

## Codebase areas involved (indicative)

- `bytes.go`: `humanateBytes`, `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`.
- `bigbytes.go`: `humanateBigBytes`, `oomm`, `BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`.
- `bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`.

## Acceptance criteria

AC1. Every example in FR1, FR2 and FR3 holds.

AC2. For every SI and IEC unit boundary reachable by each function, the smallest promoted input and the largest
input that is not promoted give the outputs required by FR1 and FR2.

AC3. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; `gofmt -l .` prints nothing.

AC4. The public API (exported names and signatures) is unchanged, and `ParseBytes` / `ParseBigBytes` still read
back every output of the five formatters to a value within one unit of the last printed digit.

## Assumptions

- "The number the function would print" is the number after the rounding each function already does: `Bytes`,
  `IBytes` and `BytesN` round half up to their number of digits, `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use Go's `%.0f` /
  `%.1f` formatting.

## Out of scope

- Any other change to formatting (number of digits, spacing, unit names) or to parsing.
- The other formatters of the module (`Comma`, `SI`, `Ftoa`, times, ordinals).
- New dependencies.

## Constraints

- The Go version declared in `go.mod`; standard library only.
- `gofmt` formatting.

   148	// ParseBigBytes parses a string representation of bytes into the number
   149	// of bytes it represents.
   150	//
   151	// See also: BigBytes, BigIBytes.
   152	//
   153	// ParseBigBytes("42 MB") -> 42000000, nil
   154	// ParseBigBytes("42 mib") -> 44040192, nil
   155	func ParseBigBytes(s string) (*big.Int, error) {
   156		lastDigit := 0
   157		hasComma := false
   158		for _, r := range s {
   159			if !(unicode.IsDigit(r) || r == '.' || r == ',') {
   160				break
   161			}
   162			if r == ',' {
   163				hasComma = true
   164			}
   165			lastDigit++
   166		}
   167	
   168		num := s[:lastDigit]
   169		if hasComma {
   170			num = strings.Replace(num, ",", "", -1)
   171		}
   172	
   173		val := &big.Rat{}
   174		_, err := fmt.Sscanf(num, "%f", val)
   175		if err != nil {
   176			return nil, err
   177		}
   178	
   179		extra := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s[lastDigit:]))
   180		if m, ok := bigBytesSizeTable[extra]; ok {
   181			mv := (&big.Rat{}).SetInt(m)
   182			val.Mul(val, mv)
   183			rv := &big.Int{}
   184			rv.Div(val.Num(), val.Denom())
   185			return rv, nil
   186		}
   187	
   188		return nil, fmt.Errorf("unhandled size name: %v", extra)
   189	}

func oomm(n, b *big.Int, maxmag int) (float64, int) {
	mag := 0

// order of magnitude (to a max order)
func oomm(n, b *big.Int, maxmag int) (float64, int) {
	mag := 0
	m := &big.Int{}
	for n.Cmp(b) >= 0 {
		n.DivMod(n, b, m)
		mag++
		if mag == maxmag && maxmag >= 0 {
			break
		}
	}
	return float64(n.Int64()) + (float64(m.Int64()) / float64(b.Int64())), mag
}

// total order of magnitude
// (same as above, but with no upper limit)
func oom(n, b *big.Int) (float64, int) {
	mag := 0
	m := &big.Int{}
	for n.Cmp(b) >= 0 {
		n.DivMod(n, b, m)
		mag++
	}
	return float64(n.Int64()) + (float64(m.Int64()) / float64(b.Int64())), mag
}

The byte formatters now move to the next unit when rounding carries the number up to the base, for example `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1.0 MB"`. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass and `gofmt -l .` prints nothing. Nothing was committed, pushed or installed.

## What changed
- **`bytes.go`, `humanateBytes`:** if the rounded number reaches the base and a larger unit exists, it prints exactly one of that unit, with the digit count that value normally gets.
- **`bigbytes.go`, `humanateBigBytes`:** same rule, using `math.RoundToEven` because that matches how `%.0f` rounds. `oomm` is untouched, and the function still works on a copy of the input.
- **Doc comments:** I added one correct example to each of the five functions. `README.markdown` showed no wrong outputs, so it is unchanged.
- **`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`:** I corrected the 12 expectations that encoded the wrong outputs, and added new tests:
    - exact boundaries for every unit, for all five functions
    - unchanged outputs
    - the last units, `QB` and `QiB`
    - the input not being modified
    - outputs parsing back within tolerance

## What I verified
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `go test -count=1 ./...` | both packages pass |
| `go vet ./...` | clean |
| `gofmt -l .` | prints nothing |
| Old code vs new code, in a scratch program outside the repo | 146,377,672 comparisons, 318,479 outputs changed, 0 illegal |
| Deliberately breaking the fix in a scratch copy, 8 ways | 6 caught by the tests, 2 not (below) |

- **Old vs new comparison:** it covered every value below 3,000,000, 3 million random values, and values around each boundary up to the `QB` range. An output could only change if the old number had reached the base and the new output equals the one-unit output.
- **The two breakages not caught:**
    - Removing the last-unit check in `humanateBytes` changes nothing, because a `uint64` can't reach 1000 EB. That check is only a safeguard.
    - The other attempt didn't compile, so it tested nothing. Removing the Big promotion entirely was caught.
- **API:** I didn't change any exported names or signatures.

## Choices where the spec was unclear
- **`IBytesN` is also fixed:** the spec lists five functions but its goal says "no byte formatter". `IBytesN` shares `humanateBytes`, so it gets the fix too, and I added a few test cases for it.
- **Very large `n` is left as it is:** at `BytesN(500_000, 309)` the rounding overflows and prints `"+Inf kB"` today. Infinity counts as "≥ base", so a plain check would have turned that into a false `1.000… MB`. I added a guard so the output stays the same, plus a test.

## Open points
- **AC4 can't hold literally for two cases, both already there before this change.** Parsing is out of scope, so I left the parsers alone, and the parse-back test allows for both:
    - `ParseBytes` truncates to whole bytes through a float, so `BytesN(1003, 6)` gives `"1.00300 kB"`, which reads back as 1002. The test's tolerance is therefore at least one byte.
    - Outputs above the `uint64` range, like `"16 EiB"`, are rejected by `ParseBytes`, and `TestByteErrors` requires that. The test skips these.
- **The top boundaries of `Bytes` and `IBytes` aren't at "boundary − 1".** Inputs pass through a `float64`, which is spaced 128 apart there, so anything within 64 of 999.5 PB (or 1023.5 PiB) already rounds onto it. The largest value not promoted is the boundary − 65, and the tests pin this.
- **Other platforms:** I only ran this on linux/amd64. These boundary tests depend on floating-point behaviour, and I didn't run them on any other architecture.
